meta.description: A science-literacy workshop: judge the quality of fictional studies with the criteria scientists use, predict the target rating and get an expert's feedback.

welcome.intro: 'Chocolate makes you smarter.' Headlines promise miracles and warn of disasters, but how good is the research behind them?
welcome.about: In this workshop you read short descriptions of studies and judge their quality with six criteria that scientists use: Title, Access, Source, Theory, Methods & Data and Conclusion.
welcome.fictional: The studies are fictional. They were written for this workshop and are modelled on the strengths and flaws of real research, but none of them describes a real study.
welcome.tasksIntro: For each study you give two answers on a scale from 1 (very low quality) to 7 (very high quality):
welcome.taskPredict: Predict the target rating. This is the answer that earns points. The target is explained below.
welcome.taskRate: Give your own rating. Judge the study yourself with the six criteria. Your own rating does not change your score, but it becomes part of the target for people who rate the study after you.
welcome.scoringTarget: Every study has a rating from an expert. The target combines that rating, counted as if {weight} people had given it, with the ratings that other participants have given the same study so far. Your own rating is never part of your target.
welcome.scoringEarly: Because the expert counts so heavily, the target stays close to the expert's rating, especially early on. Even with {count} ratings from other participants, the expert's rating makes up {share} of the target.
welcome.scoringPoints: A prediction that matches the target exactly scores 100 points. You lose {penalty} points for each point you are away from the target, so a prediction 1 point away scores {one} and one 2 points away scores {two}.
welcome.scoringFeedback: After each study you see your score, the target with how it was worked out and the expert's feedback on each of the six criteria.
welcome.leaderboardText: Your results appear on a public leaderboard under a random nickname, such as 'Curious Otter 42'. The leaderboard ranks people by their average score per study, once they have rated at least {minRank} studies.
welcome.length: There are {total} studies. You can stop and see your results at any point after rating {minFinish}.
welcome.leaderboardRoom: This session is part of the workshop room {room}. At the end you can see the leaderboard for this workshop as well as the one for everyone.
welcome.dataCollected: We store your ratings and predictions, your scores, how much weight you give each of the six criteria at the end, how long you took over each study and when you answered, together with your random nickname, the language, any workshop room code and random codes that identify this session and this browser. We do not ask for your name, email address or any other personal details.
welcome.dataNoTracking: The answers are kept in a Google Firebase database. There are no analytics or tracking cookies. Your progress is also kept in this browser's storage, so you can reload the page without losing it.
welcome.dataUse: The data are pseudonymous: the random codes link your answers to each other, not to you. By taking part you agree that your answers may be used for research on how people judge the quality of studies, and shared and analysed in anonymous form. Your nickname and scores appear on the public leaderboard and the live dashboard.

guide.heading: Before you begin
guide.intro: Take your time with the glossary and the rubric. They explain the terms in the studies and the six criteria you will judge them by. You can open both again from any study with the 'Glossary and rubric' button.
guide.glossaryIntro: Terms you will meet in the studies.
guide.rubricIntro: Use these six criteria to judge each study, then weigh them up to reach your overall rating from 1 to 7. You can give some criteria more weight than others.

results.reviewIntro: The answers for each study, in the order they were given, with the expert's feedback.
results.takeawayAccess: Open access and open data let anyone read and check the work. They are good signs, but not proof of quality on their own.
results.takeawayHype: Spotting hype: an overstated title is a warning sign, not a verdict. Check whether the methods and the conclusion support it.
results.takeawayMethods: Methods matter: the size of the sample, a fair comparison group and shared data carry much of the weight when you judge a study.
results.takeawaySource: Source credibility: predatory journals publish almost anything for a fee, and a company's own reports may have a conflict of interest.
results.takeawayConclusion: Careful conclusions: good studies say what they cannot show. Be wary of claims that go beyond the data, such as treating a link between two things as proof that one causes the other.
results.takeawayCompare: Comparing judgements: after each study you could compare your rating with the expert's and with other participants' ratings. Where they differed, the expert's notes on each criterion show what the expert weighed differently.
results.exploreIntro: When you read about research in the news:
results.exploreData: check whether the data are available
results.exploreClaims: ask whether the conclusion fits the evidence
results.exploreSource: consider who published the study and who paid for it
